articles.title: 'Unacceptable': India condemns attack on commercial vessel off Oman, 13 Indians rescued
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India on Sunday condemned an attack on the commercial vessel MT El Gaia off the coast of Oman, saying 13 of the 14 Indian crew members onbo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Sunday condemned an attack on the commercial vessel MT El Gaia off the coast of Oman, saying 13 of the 14 Indian crew members onboard had been rescued while search and rescue operations continued for the missing Indian national.The ministry of external affairs (MEA) said the Indian Embassy in Oman was closely monitoring the situation and coordinating with Omani authorities. The statement came as an Iranian cargo vessel was also reported to have been struck off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian state media reporting one death and four injuries.“We condemn the attack on the commercial vessel MT El Gaia off the coast of Oman earlier today. Of the 14 Indian crew onboard, 13 Indians have been rescued so far. Search and Rescue operations for the missing Indian national are continuing,” the MEA said.The ministry said it had reiterated India's call for immediate de-escalation and the use of dialogue and diplomacy to restore peace in the region.The MEA said the targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers, civilians and civilian infrastructure in the region was unacceptable.“We reiterate our call for immediate de-escalation of tensions and pursuance of dialogue and diplomacy to bring peace to the region. The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers, civilians, and civilian infrastructure in the region is unacceptable,” it said.India also called for the restoration of safe navigation and commercial traffic through international waterways in the region.“We also urge that free and safe navigation and flow of commerce through the international waterways in the region be restored at the earliest,” the MEA said.The Indian statement came amid renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, where an Iranian cargo vessel was reportedly struck early Sunday near Qeshm Island.Iranian state media said the attack killed one person and wounded four others. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor separately said a vessel had been hit by a projectile while transiting the strait, triggering a fire and an evacuation operation, although it was not immediately clear whether it was the same incident.Iran's state-run IRNA quoted the governor of Qeshm as blaming a “terrorist enemy” for the attack.Hours before the reported strike, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said: “Our people can’t be bullied into submission. Iran won’t surrender,” according to a social media post.The attacks came a day before a planned meeting of foreign ministers from regional countries in Oman to discuss efforts by Iran and Oman to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Iran has said that an agreement with Oman on managing the waterway would not automatically mean that the strait would be reopened to shipping. Pezeshkian told India Today TV on Saturday: “The waterway would be opened up on the condition that the U.S. will terminate its blockade.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body:
Police have released images of six men they want to speak to in connection with an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Hampshire police attended Eastney Marina on 6 September after hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

The force said several police, coastguard and Border Force vehicles had been damaged during the evening. Seven officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously hurt.

Assistant Chief Constable Tony Rowlinson urged anyone who recognised the six men to contact police.

On Friday, a 42-year-old man from Paulsgrove was charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police officer in connection with the incident. He has been remanded into custody.

A 16-year-old boy was arrested on Saturday in connection with the disorder. He has been released on bail pending further enquiries.

Around 500 anti-migrant protesters took to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday and were met by hundreds of counter-protesters from Stand up to Racism.

articles.title: In 1991, Monty Don bought a Herefordshire home with a 2-acre abandoned field; 35 years later, Longmeadow became the garden millions knew from TV
articles.summary: UK News: After 23 years at the helm, Monty Don announced that he is stepping down from the BBC’s long-running Gardeners' World series, bringing an end to one o.
articles.body: After 23 years at the helm, Monty Don announced that he is stepping down from the BBC’s long-running Gardeners' World series, bringing an end to one of the longest and most recognisable chapters in British gardening television."I have decided that the current series of Gardeners' World is to be my last," Monty Don, 71, confirmed earlier this month. The broadcaster and gardener joined the programme in 2003 and has spent the past 16 years presenting it from his 2-acre private garden, Longmeadow, transforming the once-abandoned field into the garden that millions of viewers have come to know. “I will still be gardening, dog by my side, here at Longmeadow,” he said while making the announcement.How Monty Don built Longmeadow into the world's most watched gardenIn 1991, Monty Don and his wife, Sarah, bought a Herefordshire property. At the time of the purchase, there was no garden to speak of. Just an overgrown field, builder's rubble and a single hazel tree. Most people would have hired contractors, drawn up plans and planted hedges. Don, however, chose to wait. For an entire year, he did almost nothing but observe. “I spent the next spring and summer just cutting the rough grass and clearing the rubbish. I raked every inch three times, got to know the lay of this land intimately. All the time I was planning, dreaming and drawing,” Monty Don wrote on his website.During those first months, he learned a lot about the land, which became the blueprint for Longmeadow. The northern exposure meant brutal winds from three directions. Rather than fight them, he spent autumn 1992 building defences. He knew he needed windbreaks. “I bought a hundred 6ft chestnut stakes and quartered them (chestnut cleaves beautifully down the grain) to make 400. I also bought 2,000 bean sticks and wove these between the stakes to make solid fences. The young hedging plants were then planted in the lee of the fences and grew much faster as a result,” he recalled. The planting began in earnest in 1993 and has not stopped since. “The changes have been dramatic and may seem astonishing to some. But in my mind, that early field with its pattern of woven fences protecting the little plants, so small yet filled with dreams, still remains beneath the skin, is still there beneath all the years,” he added.Longmeadow began as a private project. Don and his wife spent the first years developing the garden for themselves. He had started a gardening column and was building a reputation as someone who took both horticulture and prose seriously. Television came later. In 2003, he took over Gardeners' World as the first self-taught gardener to present it. After a stroke in 2008, he returned to the show in 2011. This time, something shifted. The show was filmed at Longmeadow itself. And just like that, his private garden became the nation's garden.Over three decades, Don and his wife transformed the 2-acre abandoned land into a series of characterful spaces: the Cottage Garden, Jewel Garden, Paradise Garden and Vegetable Garden. Millions of people watched Longmeadow change through the seasons. While some grew fond of the Jewel Garden, the spiritual centre of the entire garden, some viewers found the Cottage Garden riveting. They watched the spring bulbs emerging from the beds and the summer bringing the garden into full bloom, with roses, large-flowered clematis, iris, foxgloves, alliums and lupins crowning the borders. They watched how he pruned, how he placed colour and how his golden retriever, Nigel, became as much a fixture as the borders. The viewers resonated with him. Don told them why choosing the right plant for the right space mattered. As Monty Don leaves the show after 23 years and 700 programmes, he certainly is not leaving gardening behind. Longmeadow will continue to flourish. For Monty Don gardening is not just about beautiful gardens or growing plants. It is about the sense of purpose, freedom, and empowerment it brings. "The real importance of gardening is the empowerment that it gives people, however small or seemingly insignificant their gardens might be. It is surprising how liberating it is, if you can grow anything at all."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US scholar invited to China for academic workshop vanishes in Yunnan, later declared ‘wrongfully detained’; Trump may raise case with Xi
articles.summary: US News: Min Zin, a US scholar, is declared 'wrongfully detained' by the US State Department after vanishing in China while attending an academic workshop. His case is to be discussed by Trump and Xi Jinping.
articles.body: US citizen and Myanmar-born scholar Min Zin has been designated as “wrongfully detained” by the US State Department after he disappeared in China following a trip for an academic workshop.Zin travelled to Yunnan at the invitation of a professor to attend a workshop on economic cooperation. He arrived in Kunming on June 3 and sent his family a message saying, “Just landed in Kunming.” His family has had no direct contact with him since.Two days later, his wife Sylvia was informed by the US Consulate in Guangzhou that Zin had been detained in Yunnan, Wall Street Journal reported.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio determined that Zin was being wrongfully detained after a review of the circumstances surrounding his detention, the State Department said.The department said Zin had travelled to China to attend an academic conference at the invitation of the Chinese government. It also accused Chinese authorities of luring him to the country and said the allegations against him were unfounded.China has disputed the US characterisation. Liu Chang, a spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said Zin was being investigated for a criminal offence and that his legal rights were being protected.Zin was born in Myanmar and later moved to the US, where he became a citizen. His academic work has focused on Myanmar's democracy and ethnic conflicts and has received US government funding, a spokeswoman for his family told WSJ.He was also involved in Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy protests. Despite his background, Zin had previously travelled to China for academic events without reported problems, including a Chinese government-backed conference in October 2025.His family says he is being held under “residential surveillance” at an undisclosed location. Under the system, Chinese authorities can hold suspects at a location away from their homes for extended periods while investigating them.According to the family spokeswoman, Zin is being kept in a small room with no windows, a bed and a toilet, with the lights left on continuously. Guards are present and he is questioned for four to six hours a day.The family says Zin has not been allowed to contact relatives. He has met a US Consulate official three times for about 30 minutes each time, with Chinese officials present, and has not been permitted to discuss his case during those meetings.He appears to be in good health but has complained of knee pain, the spokeswoman said. When he is not being questioned, he reportedly spends several hours meditating.The State Department said Zin and another US citizen, Dr Youlin Chen, are currently being wrongfully detained in China.Zin's case is expected to feature among the issues raised by US President Donald Trump when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House on September 24.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body:
Europe's female golfers regained the trophy at the 20th Solheim Cup after beating defending champions the United States on Sunday.

England's Lottie Woad sealed an early triumph in Cromvoirt in the Netherlands in front of delighted fans with her win against US player Austin Kim. Europe won 15-13 overall.

German Esther Henseleit told broadcaster Sky: "It feels extremely good. Tonight will be really good. It was great fun and everyone played well."

Both teams started the 12 singles matches on the final day of the prestigious continental contest with the scores level at 8-8. Two years ago, the US team regained the Solheim Cup at home in Gainesville with a 15.5-12.5 victory over Europe.

The biennial team competition is the women's counterpart to the men's Ryder Cup.

articles.title: Russia struck train near Poland border shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials passed through
articles.summary: The former UK PM said "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning".
articles.body:
A Russian strike has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other top European officials had passed through.

No casualties were reported after the Russian strike, which hit the train's engine.

Johnson and some of Europe's most senior security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on their way back from a conference in the capital, Kyiv.

Russia said Sunday it struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but the former PM said "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning" and asked "When are we going to give them the air defences they need?"

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a Russian drone had struck 800m from Polish border.

Russia has in recent months carried out a number of deadly attacks targeting Ukraine's trains, railway depots and other transport facilities.

Earlier this month, six employees of the state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia were killed after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

This week, a female conductor died in a Russian drone attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine.

In January, President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned as "terrorism" a Russian strike on a crowded passenger train in the north-eastern Kharkiv region that left five people dead.

The Russian attacks have significantly damaged Ukraine's vast train network - the main mode of transportation for millions of Ukrainians as all air travel has been suspended since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
